notes:
I've written notes on all 23 verses, but three areas are missing. I ran out of searches before I could read any Catholic or Orthodox source (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), the NET Bible notes, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. I also found no Lutheran, Wesleyan or Pentecostal source that comments on these verses as a tradition. And I found no verse where Protestant traditions clearly disagree; the only disagreements below are between individual commentators.

## Introduction (vv. 1–5)

**v. 1**
- **Setting:** Guzik says Moses spoke with a heavy heart. He knew he would not enter Canaan with Israel, because his disobedience at Meribah (Numbers 20:1-13) meant he would not see the exodus through to the end. He also quotes Kalland: "these are the words" suggest a suzerain-vassal treaty preamble (a suzerain is an overlord king; the opening reads like the start of a treaty between a great king and a lesser one). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **"All Israel":** The Pulpit Commentary says Moses could not have been heard by the whole crowd. Jewish interpreters say he spoke to the elders, who carried his words to the people. Gill takes the same view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-1.htm
- **"Suph":** Gill says it means "opposite Suph", probably a place in Moab, perhaps the same as Suphah in Numbers 21:14, not the Red Sea. Keil and Delitzsch, by contrast, read it as still opposite to the Red Sea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-1.htm
- **The place names:** One commentary on the BibleHub page notes that Jewish commentators link these places to the people's particular sins, so naming them works as a rebuke, and that Jews call Deuteronomy "the book of reproofs." Keil and Delitzsch think the names are not exact directions; they are meant to call up to view the scene of the addresses which follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-1.htm
- **Precept Austin:** The phrase "Moses spoke" occurs 4x and in this context represents the last words Moses ever spoke. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **Modern scholarship ("beyond the Jordan"):**
  - The Gospel Coalition's introduction says the phrase means the opening is written from a standpoint *in* the land, after these events have taken place and the people have crossed the Jordan. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/
  - The Cambridge Bible says the place names cannot be harmonised with the book's repeated statement that Moses spoke in Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-1.htm Precept Austin quotes Rosscup calling this commentator a "radical liberal." https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-resources
  - Coffman defends Moses as author. He says in Deuteronomy "beyond Jordan" means the east side twelve times and the west side six times. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/deuteronomy-1.html
  - GotQuestions dates the setting to approximately 1400 BC. It says skeptics argue the book is the work of writers and editors who lived hundreds of years after Moses. https://www.gotquestions.org/when-was-Deuteronomy-written.html

**v. 2**
- **The main point:** The short trip shows that the delay was caused by banishment for their apostasy and frequent rebellions, not by distance (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown; Poole says much the same). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-2.htm
- **Distance:** Gill says this is the usual walking time, not how long Israel actually took. If a day's walk is twenty miles, the distance must be two hundred and twenty miles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-2.htm
- **Guzik:** Horeb to Kadesh took eleven days, but from Kadesh Barnea back to Kadesh Barnea took forty years. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Deu/Deu-1.cfm
- **Pulpit homiletics (J. Orr):** Sin turns short ways into long ones. https://biblehub.com/sermons/deuteronomy/1-2.htm
- **Ellicott:** He takes vv. 1–2 as an editorial introduction. In his view the material was first spoken between Sinai and Kadesh, and re-delivered in the plains of Moab. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-2.htm
- **Utley (bible.org):** The verse does not fit well between vv. 1 and 3 if it is just a travel summary. He thinks it may show the trip should have taken eleven days, but because of unbelief it took a whole generation. https://bible.org/book/export/html/20875

**v. 3**
- Benson places the speech in the plains of Moab, there being now but two months before the death of Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-1.htm
- MacArthur (quoted by Precept Austin): The years of divine judgment (Nu 14:33-34+) were ending. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62474/

**v. 4**
- Guzik takes vv. 2–4 as one unit about the journey. He says retelling it was an important testimony of God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- I found no comment on Sihon and Og themselves.

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** The name Deuteronomy means "second law." Moses repeats the law because those who heard it at Mount Sinai had died in the wilderness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Precept Austin on "undertook":** The word suggests choosing to act. In effect Moses made up his mind to expound the law. Edward Woods adds that this law was not just information; it was to be taught to each generation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

## Leaving Horeb (vv. 6–8)

**v. 6**
- **Guzik:** A year at Mount Sinai was enough; He did not bring them out of Egypt for them to live forever at Sinai.
- **Spurgeon (Baptist), as quoted by Guzik:** Some live long enough at Sinai, under the law – when they should move on to Calvary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Matthew Henry:** Though God brings his people into trouble and affliction, he knows when they have been tried long enough. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-2.htm

**v. 7**
- Jack Deere (Bible Knowledge Commentary) says these borders go beyond the territory that Israel ever actually possessed. Under David and Solomon many peoples were subjects only by paying tribute. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**v. 8**
- **Merrill:** Israel was not about to take the land of other people but to receive the land as a gift from its divine owner. He also says Occupation of the land was not an option but an edict.
- **Deere:** The command "take possession" occurs 18 times in Deut.
- **Precept Austin:** God gave the land, but Israel had to take part in possessing it. Ownership was permanent, but their right to occupy it depended on their obedience to God.
- **A dispensational view (not a tradition-wide position):** Precept Austin also says Israel will one day inherit this land fully in the Millennial reign of Christ. I found no source on the other side of this question.

All v. 8 points: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

## Appointing leaders (vv. 9–18)

**vv. 9–12**
- **Background:** Precept Austin compares Jethro's advice in Exodus 18. Moses chose able men as leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **Ellicott:** Moses' instructions are an admirable expansion, but only an expansion of Jethro's advice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/1.htm
- **Bridgeway:** Only by God's mercy did Israel enjoy just, impartial and humanitarian government. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-2.html

**vv. 13–14**
- **Matthew Henry:** We must not grudge that God's work be done by other hands than ours, provided it be done by good hands. Moses would not act without their approbation (the people's approval). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_001.cfm
- **Who chose the leaders?** When Critics Ask (quoted by Precept Austin) says the people chose and Moses appointed, So it is proper to speak of either Moses or the people as choosing the judges. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**v. 15**
- **Guzik:** The choice combined approval by the congregation, and approval by Moses himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Kalland:** The group sizes sound military, but the current need was for assistant judges, not for military men. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**vv. 16–17**
- **Gill:** judges stand in the place of God, are put into their office by him, and act under him, and for him, and are accountable to him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-17.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Judges act for God. if you judge unrighteously, you misrepresent him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/1-17.html
- **Geneva Bible note:** You are his Lieutenants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-17.htm
- **Cambridge Bible:** Moses wanted lower judges to feel that they too represent God: at every stage judgement is His. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/1-17.htm
- **Precept Austin:** The buck stops with God, not the judge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** Lack of courage leads to perversion of justice. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brv/deuteronomy/1-17.html

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin notes that the "at that time" of vv. 9, 16 and 18 preceded the departure from Horeb. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

## From Horeb to Kadesh (vv. 19–23)

**v. 19**
- What the Bible Teaches (quoted by Precept Austin) says the hard road came from obeying God by following the cloud, not from disobeying. It warns against assuming that difficulties faced by Christians are due to their disobedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary

**vv. 20–21**
- **Guzik:** This was the critical moment for Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Precept Austin:** God gave but Israel had to take. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **Wiersbe:** God's commandment is always God's enablement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62474/
- **Spurgeon (Faith's Checkbook):** He applies the verse to Christians: THERE is a heritage of grace which we ought to be bold enough to win for our possession. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62474/

**v. 22**
- **Guzik:** There was no compelling reason to send spies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Precept Austin:** Numbers 13:2 might make it look like God's idea, but sending spies was not His original plan, nor was it Moses' plan, but it was the people's plan. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **A. B. Simpson:** For a people led by God, falling back on mere human wisdom was inconsistent and dangerous. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **John Grant:** God allowed the plan anyway, so that the people could not use a refusal as an excuse for not entering the Land, and to test their faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-1-commentary
- **J. Vernon McGee:** God had already searched it out! https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62474/

**v. 23**
- **Guzik:** Moses must have remembered this with some measure of regret. In his reading the plan was first suggested by the people, then approved by Moses, then allowed and regulated by God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-1/
- **Precept Austin:** Moses would have picked the bold and fearless men from each tribe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62474/
